resources.string: Almost all scam sites live on domains that are days or hours old. Real companies have had their address for years.
Scammers rarely keep domains that long.
Young. Not proof, but a reason to look closer.
Everything before the @ is a decoy — the browser goes to what comes AFTER the @.
“{brand}” only appears BEFORE the real domain
The page belongs to {domain}, not to {brand}. The brand name up front is camouflage — the owner is always the part right before the ending.
{domain} is a different domain from {brand}’s real one. Additions like “-login”, “-service” or typos are the classic pattern.
The real server isn’t visible. Many legitimate sites use this too — on a fresh domain, though, it’s typical for scam campaigns.
No certificate in the public logs
Every https site leaves a trace there — no trace means: very new or never set up properly.
That is not an acquittal: new scam sites aren’t listed anywhere for the first hours.
Name resolution didn’t answer — this part of the check is missing.
This well-known site forwards to its encrypted version (https) – not a warning sign.
Almost every real site is encrypted today. An http link is either old or careless.
Special characters in the domain name
The name contains characters that look like Latin letters ({host}). That’s how “paypaI” with a capital i is made from “paypal”.
Bare IP address instead of a domain name
Serious providers link to their name, not to a numeric address.
{list} names other pages under this name
Single pages under this name were reported, not exactly this link. On very well-known sites that is normal (they also host other people’s content); otherwise better be careful.
{list} names the start page of this very well-known site. Such entries are old or wrong – Linkwache does not count them as a warning sign.
Long strings often contain an ID that identifies exactly you.
Words like “login”, “verify”, “vote” or “parcel” are meant to create pressure to act.
A company has mail addresses under its domain. There are none here — the domain exists only for this page.
No server behind it — either already shut down or not live yet.
Normal websites don’t need a port number in the link.
Some endings (e.g. .de) don’t publish the age.
Google Safe Browsing warns about this page
The same list that makes Chrome and Firefox show a red warning: {types}
The target is hidden. Linkwache resolves it without opening the target.
Long chains in front of the real name are meant to distract from the owner.
The ending .{tld} is popular with scammers
Cheap and anonymous to register. Companies, banks and authorities practically never use it.
Resolved without opening the target. The target is what gets judged.
Listed at URLhaus as a malware distributor
Listed at URLhaus as a malware address
According to URLhaus, exactly this address spreads malware.
The sandbox rates this page as malicious
A bank never sends links to log in. If your account really has a problem, you’ll see it in the app or on the site you type in yourself.
A parcel is supposedly stuck and a small fee will release it. The target is your card data. Track parcels only via the carrier’s own app or site that you open yourself.
“Please vote for …” → phone number → code for “Linked devices”. Whoever enters the code hands over their WhatsApp. The sender is usually hijacked already — call them.
Only open it if you expect exactly this sender and exactly this address. When in doubt, go to the company’s known site or app yourself.
A single warning sign isn’t a verdict. Check whether the sender really sent this link.
That is not an acquittal: brand-new scam sites aren’t on any list yet. Stay wary if the page asks for passwords, codes or payment details.
Don’t open it, don’t enter anything, don’t forward it. If a friend sent it: call them — their account is probably hijacked.
The saved browser is no longer installed. Choose another one.

Some apps open links in their own built-in browser instead of your default browser (for example some messengers and social networks). Those links bypass Linkwache. In such apps use “Share → Check with Linkwache”, or switch the app’s setting to open links in the default browser.
Warning with the reasons – “Open anyway” only after 3 seconds.
Opens right away – you only see a short notice.
Server not reachable – you decide, nothing opens by itself.
Blocked – opening only through a deliberate second step.
You decide whether to open it anyway.
Checking is paused – links open without a check.
The language follows your phone’s settings (Android 13 and later: per app in the system settings).
Links without warning signs open in this browser. Linkwache has preselected your current browser.
Linkwache checks this by itself when you come back.
Android asks whether Linkwache may become your default browser app. Choose Linkwache. Your real browser stays installed – Linkwache hands every checked link to it.
If no question appears: open Settings → Apps → Default apps → Browser app and choose Linkwache, then come back here.
From now on every link you tap in mail, messengers, text messages or PDFs is checked before it opens.
The public Linkwache server is preset. You only need to change this if you run your own server.
Try it with a test link
No web link found in the shared text.
Linkwache looks for a new version at most twice a day and only shows a notice here. Nothing is installed without you.
Android now asks you to confirm the update. Your settings are kept.
The download failed. Please try again later.
The download is damaged (checksum mismatch). Nothing was installed.
The download is not signed with the Linkwache key. Nothing was installed.
Android asks once whether Linkwache may install apps. This is used only for Linkwache’s own updates.
Checks every link before it opens
I know what I am doing
This link shows clear signs of a scam. Never enter passwords, codes or payment details on that page. Opening it is recorded in the local history.
This cannot be added. Special characters and IP addresses are not allowed.
Also built in: a short list of very large sites (search engines, webmail, encyclopedias).
Links to these domains open without a server check, including their subdomains. Look-alike addresses never match.
Linkwache is not the default – links bypass the check.
Linkwache is the default – links are checked.
The last 200 checks. Stored only on this phone.
While paused, links open without a check.
A random number for the server’s rate limit. It contains no personal data.
Address and path. Everything after “?” and “#” stays on your phone.
No browser found. Please install a browser first.
Links without warning signs open in this browser. Linkwache has preselected your previous default browser.
Linkwache is not the default yet. Try again, or choose Linkwache in the system settings.
No connection. Please check the address.
Please enter an https address (http only inside your home network).
The server that checks links. It only receives the address of a link – never the part after “?” or “#”.
Every link checked before it opens
Linkwache sits between your apps and your browser. Links from mail, messengers, text messages and documents are checked first; links without warning signs open right away.
Choose your browser in the settings first.
Not opened: Linkwache only opens web links (http and https).
Linkwache looks for warning signs – it cannot prove that a page is harmless.
Linkwache found warning signs. Only open this link if you expect exactly this address from exactly this sender.
The Linkwache server could not be reached, so only the local check ran. Decide yourself – nothing opens on its own.
Linkwache blocked this link. It shows clear signs of a scam.
The local check found no warning signs. That is not a full check.
There is no connection to the server.
No server address is set. Add one in the settings.
Too many checks in a short time. Please wait a moment.
The server did not answer within 6 seconds.
